T57 exists to make food trade verified, connected and financeable for every business that grows, raises, catches, processes or sells food.
The challenge
A single food trade still needs eight separate services

A single food trade still needs eight separate services
The world spends about $ 2.22 trillion a year importing food (FAO, 2025 forecast). Yet finding a buyer, checking them, agreeing terms, arranging finance, insurance, inspection, shipping and customs each come with their own paperwork, delays and risk. Banks rejected 41 % of SME trade finance applications in 2025, part of a $ 2.5 trillion global gap (ADB, 2026).
Trust
Buyers and sellers cannot easily tell who is real, who owns the goods and who is only passing them on.
Fragmentation
Quotes, contracts, inspection reports, finance and shipping documents live in different inboxes and systems, so details get lost or changed.
Access to finance
Lenders cannot see a clean, verified history of a trade, so good businesses are turned away or charged more.

FAQ
Questions we hear most

Questions we hear most
What is T57?
T57 is AI-native digital trade infrastructure for the food industry. It brings verification, quotes, contracts, finance access, insurance, inspection and logistics onto one trade record for verified members.
Who can join T57?
Any business in the food chain can apply, including farmers, fishers, processors, manufacturers, brands, traders, importers, wholesalers, supermarkets and HoReCa buyers. Every member is verified before trading.
Does T57 lend money or hold my funds?
No. T57 does not lend, hold client funds, own goods or provide transport. Finance, escrow, insurance and logistics are provided by licensed partners through the platform.
Which countries does T57 cover?
T57's founding markets are Saudi Arabia, the UAE, India, Malaysia and Türkiye. Businesses in other countries can apply for membership online.
How does T57 use AI?
AI helps with matching, risk checks, document preparation and forecasting. People make the final decisions, and any adverse decision is reviewed by a person.

The challenge
Every party sees only part of the deal

Every party sees only part of the deal
A shipment of rice or dates can pass through a farmer, a cooperative, a processor, a trader, an importer, a bank, an insurer, an inspector, a freight forwarder and a customs authority. Each sees only part of the deal, so trust is rebuilt at every step and risk builds up in the gaps. Around 13.3% of food is lost between harvest and retail (FAO, 2023), and 645 million people still went hungry in 2025 (SOFI, 2026).
Unknown counterparties
It is hard to tell producers from intermediaries, or real companies from shell companies.
Disconnected services
Finance, insurance, inspection and logistics are bought separately, with no shared view of the trade.
Uneven access
Smaller producers and SMEs struggle to reach buyers, lenders and fair terms that larger players take for granted.

Use case · Illustrative example
Indian rice reaches a Saudi distributor through a Riyadh trader

Indian rice reaches a Saudi distributor through a Riyadh trader
A Riyadh trading house agrees to supply basmati rice from an Indian processor to a Saudi distributor. On T57, all three firms hold a T57 Passport and role label, so each knows who controls the goods. The trader sends one deal file to several licensed lenders, who compete to fund the purchase. Inspection in India, freight and Saudi clearance are booked through partners. The processor, trader, distributor, lender and inspector all work from the same trade record, so documents match and payment releases when agreed milestones are met.

The problem
The food trade is drowning in data yet starving for insight

The food trade is drowning in data yet starving for insight
The global food trade runs on the illusion of efficiency. Platforms today focus on price discovery and container movements while ignoring the real bottlenecks: fragmented data, a lack of convenient funding, chronic paperwork and policy blind spots.
Governments see too late
They see disconnected snapshots of demand and supply months after the fact, with no live view of waste, surpluses and shocks across borders.
Traders work blind
PDFs, emails and static directories obscure origin, quality and risk, while duplicate audits and changing standards push compliance costs up and price out smallholders.
Producers can't get funded
Small farmers, cooperatives and agri-SMEs face a multi-trillion-dollar financing gap, while logistics, finance and agronomy are still treated as separate worlds.

How a member is verified
Business, people, documents, sanctions and site checks before anyone trades.
T57's club membership replaces anonymous, open listings with a curated, fully verified trade club, using a process that goes beyond a standard business-registry check to ensure compliance and close trades faster.
The problem
Open marketplaces: who is real?

Open marketplaces: who is real?
Without a club-based model, food and agri trade is opaque and unreliable. Traditionally, buyers have posted RFQs on marketplaces and waited days, only to receive incomplete or non-serious responses, and never knowing who is behind a profile. Sellers have struggled to distinguish genuine demand from trial inquiries, resulting in delayed or failed payments that have eroded margins and trust.
T57 changes this by determining each member's trust score through a blockchain-enabled process that evaluates document quality, business legitimacy, compliance and risk, on-field verification, trade history, financial stability, reference response, partner relationship, ecosystem reputation, and overall reputation. The evaluation is used to generate a verified T57 ID with appropriate badges and a score, giving farmers and producers, cooperatives and FPOs, buyers and importers, sellers and exporters, traders and aggregators, manufacturers and enterprises, food processors, service providers, financiers and investors, partners and collaborators, and governments and regulators a stronger basis for reducing counterparty and transaction risk.

From application to trusted trade

From application to trusted trade

Curated membership built on trust scoring
Every applicant wishing to join T57 is assessed on document quality, business legitimacy, compliance and risk, on-field verification, trade history, financial stability, reference responses, partner relationships, ecosystem reputation, and overall reputation.

When trusted capacity really matters

When trusted capacity really matters
A mid-sized, export-focused food processor in North Africa seeks to bid on a multi-year government tender for fortified wheat-based products but cannot, on its own, meet the required annual volume or the stringent delivery performance clauses. Through T57 Club Membership, the processor can access a set of pre-verified upstream mills and aggregators with documented volume histories, financial standing, and quality records.

Because all parties are already KYC/KYB-cleared and trade on the same platform, the government buyer gains greater confidence in the continuity of supply and compliance, and participating members gain access to high-quality demand that would be inaccessible in an open, uncurated marketplace.

The problem
Quotes in different formats, from suppliers you cannot check

Quotes in different formats, from suppliers you cannot check
Most food trade still starts with an enquiry sent by email, WhatsApp or a broker. Quotes come back in different formats, currencies and Incoterms, often from suppliers the buyer cannot check. Specifications get lost in long message threads, and the terms finally agreed are retyped into a contract by hand. Buyers waste days comparing offers that are not like for like. Sellers waste time answering enquiries that were never serious.
How it works
Request → Bid → Award

Request → Bid → Award
01
Request
A verified buyer sets product, grade, quantity, packaging, Incoterms, destination and delivery window once.
02
Bid
Verified suppliers matched to the request submit quotes in the same structure, so price and terms line up.
03
Award
The buyer compares bids side by side, accepts one, and the contract is generated from the accepted quote.
What makes it different
Built for trust, not just listings

Built for trust, not just listings
Only verified bidders Every supplier holds a T57 Passport and a role label (owner-producer, processor, trader or intermediary). Buyers know who they are dealing with before they read a price.
Like-for-like comparison Structured quotes and recent price data sit side by side. Buyers can see which offer is strongest and how it compares with the market.
From quote to contract with no retyping The accepted quote becomes the contract, with the same product, price, quantity and terms. Both parties work from one trade record from the first message.
Or let buyers bid Sellers can list a lot, such as premium Madinah dates, set a reserve price and a closing time, and let verified buyers bid. The best price wins, with escrow and the contract already in place.

Finance a trade
Turn a verified trade into finance offers from licensed partners, tracked to settlement.
T57 solves the finance gap for food SMEs by turning every trade into a verified, documented deal that licensed lenders can assess and fund.
The problem
Weeks of separate applications

Weeks of separate applications
The global trade finance gap reached $2.5 trillion in 2025, and banks rejected 41% of SME trade finance applications (ADB, January 2026). Food SMEs are hit hardest. Each bank asks for the same documents in a different format, takes weeks to respond and often says no because it cannot see a clean record of the trade. So producers and traders fund deals from their own cash, turn down orders or accept expensive informal credit.
How it works
Request → Compare → Fund and repay

Request → Compare → Fund and repay
01
Request
From an accepted trade, send a finance request built from your verified deal file: Passport, contract, counterparties and documents.
02
Compare
Licensed banks and finance companies, including Islamic finance providers, review the same file and compete with offers.
03
Fund and repay
Accept the best offer. At settlement, the end buyer's payment goes into escrow and repays the lender automatically.
What makes it different
Built for trust, not just listings

Built for trust, not just listings
One file, many lenders You prepare one request, not one per bank, and lenders compete for your trade.
Verified evidence Lenders see a verified business, a contract generated from an accepted quote and a full trade record, which makes it easier to say yes.
Self-liquidating structure Repayment comes from the trade itself through escrow, which lowers the risk for lenders and the burden for you.
Why lenders trust T57
Bank blockchains became digital silos. T57 shows the whole trade.

Bank blockchains became digital silos. T57 shows the whole trade.
Between 2022 and 2023, several bank-backed trade networks closed, including we.trade, Marco Polo, TradeLens and Contour. Each connected its own members and little else, so no one could see the whole trade. T57 starts from the trade, not the bank.
Every party in view A lender reviewing a $10 million deal sees the buyer, the seller, the insurer, the freight forwarder, the shipping line and the inspector, all verified and on one record.
Pay as the trade moves Smart contracts release funds at each verified milestone: loading, departure, arrival and inspection. If something goes wrong at loading, payments stop, so exposure is the first tranche, not the whole deal.
One button, every lender Tap "I need trade finance" while you buy. Partner banks, fintechs, finance companies and crowdfunding platforms are alerted at once. Both sides are already KYC and KYB checked, with banks taking part in those checks, so approval is faster and lenders compete on price.

T57 solves the problem of trade documents that can be copied, faked or pledged twice, by recording them as unique, tokenized digital assets on a tamper-evident ledger.
The problem
Paper documents can be copied and pledged twice

Paper documents can be copied and pledged twice
Trade finance still runs on paper. A bill of lading, warehouse receipt or invoice can be scanned, altered or used as collateral with more than one lender. Lenders know this, so they ask for more checks, more time and more security, and smaller businesses are often refused. The goods are real and the trade is sound, but the documents behind them are hard to trust.
How it works
Verify → Tokenize → Fund

Verify → Tokenize → Fund
01
Verify
A trade document, such as an invoice, warehouse receipt or bill of lading, is checked against the verified trade record.
02
Tokenize
The document is recorded as a unique digital token (often called an NFT) on a tamper-evident ledger, linked to its owner and the trade.
03
Fund
Licensed lenders and investors can see the token's history and fund against it. The token cannot be pledged twice, and its status updates as the trade moves.
What makes it different
Built for trust, not just listings

Built for trust, not just listings
One document, one owner Each token is unique and traceable, so the same invoice or receipt cannot be financed twice.
Linked to real trade Tokens are created only from documents on a verified T57 trade record, never from unverified paper.
Wider funding Verified, traceable documents can attract banks, finance companies and, where the law allows, institutional investors.

When the goods are sold, the token's status updates and the lender is repaid from the sale.

We believe that a real asset should be easy to prove and fair to finance.

T57 solves the standoff between buyers who will not pay first and sellers who will not ship first, by holding payment with a licensed escrow partner until agreed milestones are met.
The problem
Buyer and seller both carry the risk

Buyer and seller both carry the risk
In food trade, someone always carries the risk. If the buyer pays upfront, it risks fraud, short shipment or poor quality. If the seller ships first, it risks late payment or no payment at all. Letters of credit solve this for some deals, but they can be costly and slow for smaller trades and domestic wholesale. Without a trusted middle ground, many good deals never happen.
How it works
Agree milestones → Fund escrow → Release

Agree milestones → Fund escrow → Release
01
Agree milestones
Buyer and seller agree when funds are released, for example on passed inspection, shipment or delivery, as part of the contract.
02
Fund escrow
The buyer pays into escrow with a licensed partner. The seller can see that the money is there before it ships.
03
Release
As each milestone is recorded on the trade record, funds are released, in part or in full. If there is a dispute, release pauses until it is resolved.

Built for trust, not just listings

Built for trust, not just listings
Milestones tied to evidence Release is linked to recorded events, such as an inspection report or delivery confirmation, on the same trade record.
Partial release and dispute triggers Funds can be released in stages, and a dispute stops release automatically until it is settled.
Works with finance Escrow can repay a lender at settlement, which makes trade finance safer and easier to get.

The problem
Eight services, eight copies of the deal

Eight services, eight copies of the deal
A single food trade still needs eight separate services. Someone has to find and check the counterparty, agree the price and terms, arrange finance, protect the payment, insure the cargo, inspect the goods, ship them and clear customs. Today each is bought separately, with its own paperwork and its own view of the deal. Details are retyped, documents drift out of line, and nobody sees the whole trade. That is why banks rejected 41% of SME trade finance applications in 2025 (ADB, January 2026), and why so many good food trades stall between agreement and delivery. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Disconnected services
Finance, insurance, inspection and logistics providers each work from their own copy of the deal.
Repeated work
The same product, price and party details are typed again and again, and every retyping risks an error.
No single view
Buyers, sellers, lenders and regulators cannot see where a trade stands or trust that its records are complete.

T57 solves the problem of food whose origin and journey cannot be proven, by linking every lot to its source, processing, shipment and documents on a tamper-evident record.
The problem
Origin and journey that cannot be proven

Origin and journey that cannot be proven
Buyers, regulators and consumers increasingly want to know exactly where food comes from: which farm or fishery, which processor, whether it is halal, organic or deforestation-free, and how it was stored and shipped. Large importers and retailers now ask suppliers for this proof as a condition of buying. Most food SMEs keep this information on paper or in separate systems, so they cannot answer quickly or convincingly, and a single food safety incident can lead to a costly, oversized recall. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Origin claims you cannot prove
Certificates and declarations are easy to copy and hard to check.
Slow, broad recalls
Without lot-level records, a problem in one batch can force a recall of far more product.
Market access at risk
Buyers and regulators may refuse goods that lack traceability records.
How T57 works for you
Register the source → Record each step → Anchor the evidence → Share proof

Register the source → Record each step → Anchor the evidence → Share proof
01
Register the source
Record the farm, fishery or factory behind each lot, linked to the producer's verified T57 Passport.
02
Record each step
Processing, packing, storage, inspection and shipment events are added to the lot's record by the parties who handle it.
03
Anchor the evidence
Key events and certificates are anchored on a tamper-evident ledger.
04
Share proof
Give buyers, auditors and regulators access to the lot's history, or share a traceability link or QR code.
Features
7 features, one trade record

7 features, one trade record
Lot-level records Each lot carries its own history from source to buyer. For processors, this makes targeted recalls possible.
Verified origins Sources are tied to verified producers with role labels. For buyers, this confirms who really grew, raised or caught the product.
Certificate linking Halal, organic, phytosanitary and food safety certificates attached to the lots they cover. For exporters, this answers buyer questions at once.
Event recording Processing, cold storage, inspection and loading events added by the parties involved. For quality teams, this shows how food was handled.
Tamper-evident ledger Key records anchored on a blockchain ledger. For regulators, this means records cannot be quietly changed.
Shareable proof Traceability links and QR codes for buyers, retailers and consumers. For brands, this turns provenance into a selling point.
Recall support Identify every buyer and shipment that received an affected lot. For food safety teams, this speeds up response.
Details that travel with the lot The product details agreed in the contract, from origin and inputs to processing, stay attached to the lot on its trade record. For buyers and regulators, this means proof of what was sold.

Who adds information to a lot's record?

T57 solves the payment risk at the heart of food trade, by connecting escrow, wallets and electronic letters of credit from licensed partners to one verified trade record.
The problem
Someone always carries the payment risk

Someone always carries the payment risk
Every food trade comes down to one question: who goes first? Buyers fear paying for goods that never arrive or arrive short. Sellers fear shipping goods that are never paid for. Traditional answers, such as advance payment, open account or paper letters of credit, either put all the risk on one side or are too slow and costly for smaller trades. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
One-sided risk
Advance payment and open account leave one party fully exposed.
Slow, paper-heavy protection
Paper letters of credit take days, and document mismatches delay payment.
Payments cut off from the trade
Money moves in one system and goods in another, so disputes are hard to settle.

Choose the protection → Fund it → Link to milestones → Settle

Choose the protection → Fund it → Link to milestones → Settle
01
Choose the protection
Pick escrow, an electronic LC or a direct wallet payment when you agree the contract.
02
Fund it
The buyer funds escrow or applies for the LC through a licensed partner.
03
Link to milestones
Release conditions, such as inspection, shipment or delivery, are tied to events on the trade record.
04
Settle
Funds are released as milestones are met, and every payment is recorded against the contract.

Trust and payments capabilities

Which payment option should I choose?
Escrow suits most new relationships and domestic wholesale. eLCs suit larger cross-border trades where a bank guarantee is expected. Wallet payments suit trusted, repeat relationships.

T57 solves the risk of paying too early or shipping too soon, by holding buyer funds with a licensed escrow partner and releasing them only when agreed, recorded milestones are met.
The problem
Paying too early or shipping too soon

Paying too early or shipping too soon
In food trade, the gap between payment and delivery is where most disputes and losses happen. A buyer pays a deposit and the goods arrive late, short or below grade. A seller ships and the buyer delays payment or disputes quality to renegotiate. Without a neutral party holding the money and clear rules for releasing it, the weaker side usually loses. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Advance-payment fraud
Buyers lose deposits to suppliers who do not deliver, or deliver something else.
Non-payment
Sellers ship and then chase payment for weeks or months.
Quality disputes
Without agreed evidence, arguments about grade or quantity drag on.
How T57 works for you
Agree release terms → Fund escrow → Record milestones → Release or pause

Agree release terms → Fund escrow → Record milestones → Release or pause
01
Agree release terms
Set milestones and release percentages in the contract, such as deposit on signing, part on inspection and balance on delivery.
02
Fund escrow
The buyer pays into an escrow account held by a licensed partner. The seller sees confirmation before it ships.
03
Record milestones
Inspection reports, bills of lading and delivery confirmations are added to the trade record.
04
Release or pause
Funds release automatically when each milestone is recorded. If either party raises a dispute, release pauses until it is resolved.

T57 solves the delays and discrepancies of paper letters of credit, by building each LC from the verified contract and connecting applicants, banks and beneficiaries on one digital record.
The problem
Paper LCs: slow and error-prone

Paper LCs: slow and error-prone
Letters of credit protect both sides of a cross-border trade: the seller is paid if it presents the right documents, and the buyer pays only if those documents are presented. But the process is slow. Applications are filled in by hand, terms are copied from contracts, and documents travel by courier between banks. When the documents do not exactly match the LC, payment is delayed. Laws such as the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records and the UK Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023 now recognize electronic trade documents, but most food SMEs still work on paper. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Slow issuance
Manual applications and bank processes take days.
Discrepancies
Small differences between the LC, the contract and the shipping documents delay payment.
Paper and couriers
Physical documents add cost and time, and can be lost or altered.
How T57 works for you
Apply from the contract → Bank approval → Issue → Present and pay

Apply from the contract → Bank approval → Issue → Present and pay
01
Apply from the contract
The buyer starts the LC application from the accepted contract, so product, quantity, price, Incoterms and dates are already filled in.
02
Bank approval
A partner bank reviews the application with the verified trade record and approves it under its own credit rules.
03
Issue
Once approved, the eLC is targeted to be issued in about 15 minutes and is visible to the seller and its bank on T57.
04
Present and pay
The seller presents shipping, inspection and insurance documents digitally. AI checks them against the LC first, and the bank pays on compliant presentation.

Contract-to-LC builder The LC application is filled in from the contract. For importers, this saves time and reduces errors.

Fast issuance About 15 minutes from approval to issuance as the target. For exporters, this means shipping sooner.
Pre-presentation checks AI compares documents with LC terms and flags discrepancies before presentation. For exporters, this means fewer rejected presentations.
Digital presentation Documents are presented on the trade record, where the law recognizes electronic documents. For both banks, this removes couriers.
Amendments on record LC amendments are requested, approved and recorded digitally. For both parties, this keeps one version of the truth.
Linked finance LCs can be combined with pre-shipment or post-shipment finance on the same record. For exporters, this unlocks working capital.
Status tracking Every step, from application to payment, is visible to authorized parties. For finance teams, this ends chasing banks by email.

Food crossing a border needs a stack of documents: commercial invoice, packing list, certificate of origin, health, phytosanitary and halal certificates, import permits and the customs declaration. Each must match the others exactly. One wrong HS code, weight or date can hold a container for days, and for chilled or frozen food every day costs money and quality. The WTO estimated that full implementation of its Trade Facilitation Agreement could cut trade costs by an average of 14.3% (WTO, World Trade Report 2015). Much of that saving comes from simpler, digital border procedures. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Inconsistent documents
The same data is typed into many documents by different parties, creating mismatches.
Classification errors
Wrong HS codes lead to delays, penalties or the wrong duty.
Late submission
Documents reach customs only when the goods arrive, so clearance starts late.

How dispute resolution works
Raise → Pause → Review → Resolve

Raise → Pause → Review → Resolve
01
Raise
Either party opens a dispute on the trade record, stating the issue, such as quality, quantity, delay or documents.
02
Pause
Where the trade uses escrow, the licensed escrow partner holds the disputed amount, and partial release is possible for any undisputed part.
03
Review
Both sides add evidence, such as inspection reports, photos and logs, to the record. T57 helps the parties reach an agreement based on the agreed terms.
04
Resolve
The parties settle, or the dispute moves to the route set in their contract. The outcome is recorded, and escrow is released accordingly.

Saudi Arabia ↔ India Rice, spices, fresh produce and meat to the Kingdom; Saudi dates and processed food to India.

Saudi Arabia ↔ Türkiye Fruit, nuts, vegetables and pasta to the Kingdom; Saudi dates and dairy to Türkiye.
UAE ↔ all markets Imports from India, Malaysia and Türkiye for the UAE and for re-export, and UAE re-exports onward.
India ↔ Malaysia ↔ Türkiye Spices, rice, palm products, pulses, nuts and processed food moving between producing markets.

T57 exists to make halal food trade across OIC member countries faster, safer and easier to verify, from certified producer to final buyer.
The challenge
The challenge

The challenge
Muslim consumers spent an estimated $1.5 trillion on food in 2024, and that figure is projected to reach $2.1 trillion by 2029 (DinarStandard, State of the Global Islamic Economy 2025/26). Yet trade between OIC countries still struggles with fragmented halal certification, limited trust between new partners, and producers who cannot reach buyers or finance in other member states. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Halal assurance
Buyers need proof that certificates are genuine, current and recognized in their market.
Limited intra-OIC links
Producers and buyers in member countries often trade through distant intermediaries.
Access to finance
Small producers and traders lack finance, including Shariah-compliant options.

T57 connects ASEAN food producers and traders, starting from Malaysia, to verified buyers in the Gulf, India and Türkiye, on a trade record built for digital trade rules.
The challenge
The challenge

The challenge
Southeast Asia is a major supplier of rice, palm oil, seafood, fruit and halal processed food. ASEAN is also moving toward common digital trade rules: negotiations on the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) concluded in May 2026, with signing targeted for November 2026. Yet many ASEAN producers still rely on intermediaries to reach distant buyers, and cross-border paperwork remains slow. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Distance from buyers
Producers rarely deal directly with buyers in the Gulf or South Asia.
Paper-based trade
Documents still move by courier and email.
Finance gaps
Small exporters struggle to fund orders while they wait for payment.

The challenge
The challenge

The challenge
The UAE is one of the world's great trading hubs: its non-oil foreign trade reached about AED 3.8 trillion ($1.03 trillion) in 2025, up about 27% on the year before (WAM). It imports most of its food, and its traders supply markets across the Gulf, Africa and Asia. Speed and trust matter, because food is perishable and margins are thin. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Supplier risk
Importers need verified suppliers and alternative origins at short notice.
Working capital
Traders tie up cash in goods in transit.
Document load
Re-exports multiply the documents and checks each shipment needs.

The challenge
The challenge

The challenge
India is one of the world's largest food producers, and its agricultural exports reached $52.55 billion in FY2025–26 (Ministry of Commerce and Industry). Yet most of its farms are small, and many producers still sell through layers of intermediaries, with little view of the final price, limited access to export buyers and little working capital. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Distance from buyers
Farmers and FPOs rarely deal directly with business buyers or importers.
Proof of quality and origin
Overseas buyers need verified suppliers and documents they can trust.
Working capital
Small exporters wait months to be paid.

Why pricing matters

Why pricing matters
Food businesses already pay for trade in many hidden ways: agents' margins, repeated document checks, bank charges, failed shipments and time spent chasing partners. Many platforms add listing fees or charge for leads that never become trades. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Hidden costs
Middlemen's margins and repeated paperwork that never appear on an invoice.
Paying for nothing
Fees for listings and leads that do not lead to trade.
One size for all
Pricing that ignores the size of the business and the market it works in.

The problem

Every country's priorities are different.
One ministry of agriculture wants its farmers and cooperatives to reach new buyers. Another ministry wants to grow food manufacturing, or develop small businesses. A food-security agency needs early warning of supply shocks. Public procurement needs clean, traceable tenders. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Late information
Food-security decisions made on old, aggregate data.
Excluded producers
Smallholders, cooperatives and small businesses left outside formal trade and finance.
Opaque procurement
Large food tenders exposed to leakage, fraud, delays and quality failures.

What governments can do on T57
Programs that fit national plans

Programs that fit national plans Subsidized memberships A ministry subscribes on behalf of farmers, cooperatives or SMEs, as a direct form of support. For governments, this means measurable reach. Programs by priority Producer inclusion, investment in food manufacturing, SME development and export growth. For ministries, this means programs that fit national plans. Public tenders, local and global Publish food tenders on T57, invite verified suppliers from home or abroad, and evaluate, award and pay on one traceable record, with escrow through licensed partners. For procurement teams, this means clean, auditable buying. Government module Food-security dashboards and index, supply status and surplus or deficit by origin, AI early warning, and scenario modeling for tariffs, quotas, subsidies and stocks. For agencies, this means seeing shocks in days, not months. Government-to-government trade Supply arrangements and emergency corridors between states, on the same verified record. For ministries, this means faster agreements. Co-funded programs with development partners Programs can be designed with multilateral development banks, UN agencies and agricultural development funds. T57 is in discussions with the World Bank and the African Development Bank. For partners, this means verified, measurable impact. Permissioned data only No individual member data is shared without consent.

Plain-language answers about T57, and the trade, finance and technology terms behind it, from escrow to HS codes.
Glossary
26 terms, in plain language

26 terms, in plain language Filter terms AI advises, people decide T57's principle for AI. AI makes recommendations, and a person reviews every adverse decision, with a stated reason and a route to contest it. On T57 → Beneficial owner The person who ultimately owns or controls a company, even if the shares are held through other companies. Bill of lading (B/L) A document issued by a carrier that receipts the goods, sets out the terms of carriage and, in most forms, gives title to the goods. Certificate of origin A document that states the country where goods were produced, used to apply duties and trade agreements. Cold chain Temperature-controlled storage and transport that keeps perishable food safe from producer to buyer. Cooperative / FPO A group of producers that sells, buys or works together. In India, a farmer producer organization (FPO) is a registered group of farmers. Corridor A regular trade route between a supplying market and a buying market, such as India to Saudi Arabia. On T57 → Escrow An arrangement where a licensed third party holds the buyer's payment and releases it to the seller when agreed conditions are met. On T57 → Halal certificate A certificate from an accredited halal body confirming that a product meets Islamic dietary requirements. On T57 → HoReCa Hotels, restaurants and caterers, the food service sector. HS code
26 terms, in plain language

The Harmonized System code that classifies traded goods for customs and duties. Incoterms Standard trade terms from the International Chamber of Commerce, such as FOB or CIF, that set who pays for and bears the risk of each stage of delivery. Intermediary A business that connects buyers and sellers without producing, processing or holding the goods. T57 labels intermediaries so buyers know who they deal with. Invoice financing Finance a lender provides against an unpaid invoice, so the seller is paid before the buyer's payment is due. KYB (Know Your Business) Checks that confirm a company is real, properly registered and licensed, and who owns it. On T57 → KYC (Know Your Customer) Checks that confirm the identity of the people who own and act for a business. On T57 → Letter of credit (LC) A bank's promise to pay the seller when the seller presents documents that meet the LC's terms. On T57 → Owner-producer A member that grows, raises, catches or makes the goods it sells, with ownership verified by T57. Phytosanitary certificate A government certificate confirming that plants or plant products meet the importing country's plant health rules. Sanctions screening Checking people and companies against government sanctions and watchlists. On T57 → Smart contract
26 terms, in plain language

Software that carries out agreed steps automatically, such as instructing a payment partner to release funds when a delivery is confirmed. Supply status by origin T57's view of whether supply of a product from an origin is surplus, stable, at risk or in shortage. On T57 → T57 Passport A member's reusable verified profile, showing their role, checks passed and trade history, shared with consent. On T57 → Tokenized trade document A trade document, such as an invoice or warehouse receipt, issued as a unique digital token so it cannot be duplicated or financed twice. On T57 → Trade finance gap The value of trade finance that businesses request but cannot get. The Asian Development Bank estimated it at $2.5 trillion in 2025. On T57 → Trade record The single shared record of a trade on T57, from quote to settlement, that every party sees. On T57 → FAQ
Common questions

Common questions
What is T57?
T57 is AI-native digital trade infrastructure for the entire food ecosystem. It is a members-only trade club where verified producers, processors, traders and buyers trade on one shared record, with finance, insurance, logistics and inspection from licensed partners.
Is T57 a marketplace?
No. On an open marketplace, anyone can list. On T57, every member is verified before they trade, and their role is checked and shown.
Does T57 buy or sell food?
No. T57 does not own goods, lend money, hold client funds or provide transport. Members trade with each other, and licensed partners provide regulated services.
Which countries does T57 operate in?
Saudi Arabia, the UAE, India, Malaysia and Türkiye, with more markets to follow.

How long does the free trial last?
Founding members get 90 days free at launch. After the launch period, the trial is 14 days.
Can I trade during the free trial?
You can explore members, intelligence and AI tools, and send requests for quote. Contracts, escrow and finance start once you subscribe and are verified.
How do I cancel or change my plan?
From your account settings. Upgrades apply at once, and downgrades apply at renewal.
Does T57 hold my money?
No. Payments, escrow and letters of credit are handled by licensed partners.
Can other members see my prices?
No. Only the parties you quote can see your prices.

The problem
T57 does not lend, hold client funds, own goods or provide transport.

T57 does not lend, hold client funds, own goods or provide transport.
It connects the specialists who do. For partners, the challenge is reaching good customers in food trade at a cost that works. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Costly customer acquisition
Finding and checking smaller food businesses one by one is expensive.
Poor data
Banks and insurers lack reliable records to price risk.
Disconnected workflows
Partners receive documents by email and re-key them.
Partner types
Four kinds of specialist, one trade record

Financial services Banks, finance companies, escrow providers, insurers and takaful operators. Logistics and inspection Freight forwarders, shipping lines, cold chain, warehouses, inspection and testing, customs brokers. Technology Cloud, data, AI, identity and integration partners. Institutions Governments, development partners and regional organizations such as the Islamic Organization for Food Security (IOFS). Research and universities Agricultural universities, research institutes and their start-ups, bringing science to farmers.

The problem
Research that never reaches the field

Research that never reaches the field
Universities and research institutes develop better seeds, breeds, practices and machines every year. Too little of it reaches the small farms and food SMEs that produce most of the world's food. Extension services are thin, results are published in forms farmers cannot use, and scientists see little reward when their work is adopted. Meanwhile, 13.3% of food is lost between harvest and retail (FAO, 2023), often for want of simple, affordable technology. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Hard to reach farmers
Findings stay in papers and stations, far from the people who could use them.
Weak commercialization
Few research results are licensed, sold or scaled, so good inventions stay local.
No proof of impact
Institutions struggle to show how their research changed yields, losses or incomes.

Our story
One question, asked in more than 60 countries

One question, asked in more than 60 countries
T57 began with one question: why does food that exists not reach the people and markets that need it? Through AlMukarramah, T57's founding team designed the strategy and ecosystem of the Islamic Organization for Food Security (IOFS), the OIC's food security institution. Over four years, the team traveled to more than 60 countries and met ministries, buyers, sellers, processors, cooperatives and farmers. Producers, traders and governments were rarely short of food or of willing partners. They were short of three things:
Access to markets
Producers and small traders cannot reach or prove themselves to buyers beyond their own networks.
Access to technology
Trade still runs on phone calls, messages and paper, with no shared record of a deal.
Access to finance
Working capital rarely reaches the smaller businesses that need it most.

Make food security visible, verifiable and actionable.

Make food security visible, verifiable and actionable.
Verified supply across borders, supply status by origin, AI early warning and a government module, in one system.
Sellers publish produce, volumes and harvest windows once, and verified buyers find them.
T57 strengthens food security by connecting verified producers and buyers across borders, and by turning verified trade data into early warning of where supply is at risk.
The problem
Import-dependent countries are exposed

Import-dependent countries are exposed
645M people faced hunger in 2025 (SOFI 2026)
136.0 FAO Food Price Index, September 2026, up 5.8% on a year earlier
20–45% of key agrifood inputs pass through the Strait of Hormuz (FAO, April 2026)
In 2025, 645 million people faced hunger, and about 520 million are still projected to in 2030 (SOFI 2026). The FAO Food Price Index reached 136.0 in September 2026, 5.8% higher than a year earlier and the highest since November 2022. Import-dependent countries are exposed: in April 2026, FAO warned that 20 to 45% of key agrifood inputs depend on passage through the Strait of Hormuz. The key challenges T57 addresses include:
Late information
Governments see supply problems only after prices rise.
Narrow sourcing
Importers depend on a few origins and intermediaries.
Excluded producers
Small producers cannot reach the markets that need their food.
How T57 supports food security
Connect, see, act, include

Verified producers in surplus regions meet verified buyers in import-dependent markets.
02

Verified trades build a live view of supply by origin: surplus, stable, at risk or shortage.
03
Act early
When an origin is at risk, buyers find verified alternative suppliers and routes.
04
Include small producers
Cooperatives and smallholders join through assisted onboarding, adding supply and earning more.

Marketing a System, Not a Product: Designing Trade Infrastructure for Multi-Party Value

Marketing a System, Not a Product: Designing Trade Infrastructure for Multi-Party Value
Why verification and trust, not vendor promises, are what a trade platform really sells.
Umme Habeeba Khanum Chief Marketing Officer
13 Jul 2026 4 min read
When I am talking to a government procurement authority, a farming cooperative, a multinational buyer, or a bank in an emerging market, I'm not pitching a software platform. I'm architecting trust across four distinct capital flows that have never had reason to operate in alignment.
This is the fundamental difference between marketing a product and marketing a system.
A product has features. You list them, you differentiate on speed, cost, or interface. By contrast, a system orchestrates behavior. It changes how multiple parties see each other, transact, and compound value together. T57 —a system disrupting the farm-to-fork economy with the world’s first AI-native food ecosystem—operates at a system level. If we showcase it as anything less, we've shortchanged ourselves.
Can we avoid the product marketing trap?

Can we avoid the product marketing trap?
Let's start where most technology CMOs stumble: feature enumeration.
I could say T57​ has "embedded digital banking," "smart contract-based escrow," and "AI-driven commodity forecasting." All true. None of it lands with a cooperative wondering if its harvest will reach a buyer in the Emirates at the contracted price. None of it persuades a government official who's been burned by 15 "revolutionary" agritech startups that promised supply chain transparency. And none of it moves capital from a development bank that sees 100 pitches a year and needs to deploy billions in loans.
Features answer the question "what does it do?" Systems answer, "Why should fundamentally different economic actors trust it?"
When T57's infrastructure enables a farming collective in India to lock in export pricing with a buyer in Dubai, hedge that position through a contract verified by distributed ledger technology, and access trade financing from a bank that would otherwise never see their cooperative balance sheet—that's not a feature. That's a permission structure. It's an entirely new infrastructure layer for global food trade. We don't sell that as a product at T57; we think of it as a treaty among commercial partners.
The key pillar of systems marketing: Verification, clarity, and alignment

The key pillar of systems marketing: Verification, clarity, and alignment In opaque commodity markets—and in agricultural trade across nations that span multiple regulatory jurisdictions and financial systems—trust lies in verification, not in vendor promises. For most of my life, as a marketing professional in technology companies, I’ve thought of marketing as focusing on “features,” “solutions,” and “offerings.” Now, I am reframing my goal to market verification and trust as the product. It’s interesting and challenging and infinitely more rewarding. As a system, T57​ makes a radical difference. That is why we don’t lead with a "Our AI predicts commodity yields with 94% accuracy." Instead, our story is: "Here's how we make it easy to move produce legally and with commercial viability across a variety of jurisdictions and compliance frameworks.” The smart contracts on T57​ don't just execute transactions; they create an immutable audit trail that simultaneously satisfies a farming cooperative in India, a government trade authority in Dubai, a compliance officer in Abu Dhabi, and a South African bank's credit committee. Verification becomes the product. The technology is merely the mechanism. For government authorities, the picture is complex.
The key pillar of systems marketing: Verification, clarity, and alignment

A government procurement officer doesn't think, "I want AI." He thinks "I need to move 100,000 tons of wheat into our corridor efficiently, and I don't know where the optimal supply points are—or whether brokers are pricing honestly." This need has made T57's mapping of surpluses, deficits, and logistics a quantifiable engineering problem.
What is systems thinking in practice?

What is systems thinking in practice? Systems thinking is what brings these actors—government procurement authority, a farming cooperative, a multinational buyer, or a bank in an emerging market—together. For T57, the farming cooperative needs the corporate buyer to commit to volume. The buyer needs supply certainty from multiple cooperatives. The government authority needs both parties to operate within its trade corridors. And the bank needs all three to generate verifiable, predictable cash flows. These interests compound. They are mutually reinforcing only if architected correctly. And T57 does precisely that. For T57, verification serves as the common language across compliance, commercial law, banking regulation, and cooperative governance. I think of it as the element that makes trust scalable. Which brings me back to my training, much of which I need to unlearn! I have to resist the feature-first storytelling that had become a natural part of my life as a marketing professional for a technology major. The temptation to lead with "We use AI and blockchain" is overwhelming. It signals technological sophistication. But now I resist it. I now lead with the problem these technologies solve together. The magic of T57 isn't in any one component. It is in how they orchestrate the flow of value. When we do that, we don’t just win markets; we expand them. Written by

The Day Our MoUs and LoIs Turned Into a Learning Machine

The Day Our MoUs and LoIs Turned Into a Learning Machine
How early MoU and LoI partners became co-designers, with pilots tied to measurable outcomes.
Mohammed Umair Chief Sales Officer
3 Jun 2026 6 min read
My core business is not collecting MoUs!
I am in the business of building a learning sales engine that turns every market signal into sharper execution for T57.
At Gulfood 2026, T57 signed over 150 MoUs and LoIs with institutional buyers across dairy, retail, manufacturing, and specialty foods. As a practical sales professional, I know that not all 150 will convert to paying clients. But each one of those signatures matters because they are live data points. They are evidence of who feels the pain most acutely, who is ready to move fastest, and where our go-to-market strategy should focus over the next 12–18 months. As head of sales, my job is to read those signals and tune the T57 sales machine.
The real message behind 150 MoUs and LoIs

The real message behind 150 MoUs and LoIs
On the surface, an MoU or an LoI is a simple document. It is a statement of intent to explore pilots and partnerships once our platform is live. Beneath the surface, it encodes a complex decision-making journey. For a cautious, committee-driven institution to sign an MoU or LoI, several things have already happened: someone has acknowledged a real problem, internal champions have been identified, legal and leadership have weighed in, and there is a shared belief that T57 can be part of the solution.
When I looked across the MoUs and LoIs we signed at Gulfood, I didn’t see a vanity metric. I saw patterns emerging from the noise. Certain categories, such as dairy and private-label manufacturing, leaned in faster than others. Some geographies pushed aggressively for early pilots and beta access, while others preferred to watch and learn before committing to next steps. A distinct subset of buyers consistently framed T57 not as ‘another tool’ but as ‘infrastructure we’ve been waiting for.’ Those patterns are our first dataset. They tell me where urgency is highest and where our value proposition lies without a long education cycle. That, in turn, shapes everything—from which accounts we prioritize to how we resource the first wave of implementations.
From static funnel to feedback loop

From static funnel to feedback loop
Traditional B2B sales views the funnel as a one-way street: leads enter at the top, revenue exits at the bottom, and conversion rates are the key performance metric. At T57, we treat the funnel as a feedback loop, not a conveyor belt. The goal is to ensure that every interaction with a MoU and LoI signatory improves our ability to serve the next one.
In practice, we treat each MoU and LoI as a learning contract long before they become commercial contracts. Before a single dollar of revenue is booked, we already track who responds fastest, who invites more stakeholders into the conversation, and who pushes for specific features or workflows. Our CRM is not just a repository of contacts; it is where we tag and cluster MoU and LoI signatories by category and problem statement. That clustering feeds directly into our product roadmap, content strategy, and partner conversations. Every pilot we schedule with these early institutions is designed to surface specific insights.
We uncover what slows onboarding, which roles inside the customer organization become internal champions, and where we encounter resistance or friction. The ‘output’ of the funnel is not only revenue; it is understanding. The more we learn, the more precise our targeting and messaging become, and the faster we can move the next wave of prospects from curiosity to conviction.
Rewriting our ideal customer profile in real time

Rewriting our ideal customer profile in real time
Before Gulfood 2026, we had a clear hypothesis about our ideal customer profile. We believed that institutions with cross-border exposure (too much paperwork, too many variables), complex compliance needs, and fragmented systems would feel the pain most acutely. Gulfood validated that thesis and sharpened it in unexpected ways. Some organizations matched our original ICP perfectly on paper, yet moved slowly in practice. Others who initially looked like edge cases became our most enthusiastic MoU and LoI signatories and pushed hardest for early access.
Instead of clinging to the old ICP, we are rewriting it in real time based on observed behavior. We now score accounts not just on size or geography but on demonstrated urgency and internal alignment. We give extra weight to signals such as a CFO joining early conversations or a regulatory team requesting dedicated workshops, because these correlate strongly with serious, sustained intent. Our segmentation is evolving so that our first 12–18 months focus on clusters of institutions and corridors where that urgency and alignment already exist. For potential partners in the food ecosystem, it means that when we come with a joint offering, we are not guessing; we are bringing a tested understanding of who adopts fastest and where network effects will be strongest.
Turning early adopters into co-designers

Turning early adopters into co-designers
A learning sales engine doesn’t stop at closing customers; it turns them into co-designers of the future. With our early MoU and LoI partners, we are deliberately blurring the line between buyer and co-creator. We are inviting operational teams, not just executives, into discovery sessions so the workflows we design reflect the messiness and constraints of real-world operations. We are structuring pilots around a small set of measurable outcomes, such as reductions in cycle time and error rates, or in compliance readiness, rather than vague promises of digital transformation.
This is good product practice; more importantly, it is a deliberate sales strategy. When early adopters see their fingerprints on the platform, they become internal champions and external advocates. They help shorten sales cycles within their own organizations and across their networks, and they become the reference points that de-risk decisions for the next wave of institutions.
Why this should matter to partners and investors

Why this should matter to partners and investors If you are a potential partner in the food space, whether you operate in procurement, logistics, finance, compliance, or category management, our approach should tell you something important: we are not spraying and praying. We are instrumenting the entire journey from the first conversation to long-term value. We are building a sales engine that starts with demonstrated intent, not wishful thinking, and uses every interaction to sharpen our view of where the market is truly ready for change. It then converts early demand into a structured learning program, making the next set of deals faster and more predictable. We are not optimizing for a noisy launch with shallow adoption that looks good for a quarter and then plateaus. We are optimizing for compounding traction built on real signals from institutions, even before our platform goes live. Gulfood 2026 was our first large-scale test of this philosophy. The 150-plus MoUs and LoIs we signed are not the finish line; they are the training data. As the head of sales, I am not chasing a perfect funnel diagram. I am building a system that learns faster than the market changes. And, in a sector as critical and complex as global food trade, that is how you get off to a flying start and stay ahead. Mohammed Umair Chief Sales Officer

As the head of sales at T57, I am used to living in the world of probabilities: outreach, response, qualification, negotiation, and, finally, revenue. Earlier this January, at Gulfood 2026, where our founder, chairman, and head of strategy, Afzal Hussain Mohammed Nakheeb, was a speaker, that probability curve bent in our favor in a way that is both unusual for a yet-to-be-launched platform and deeply revealing about how the global food trade wants to buy technology.
What 150 MoUs and LoIs really signal

What 150 MoUs and LoIs really signal
During Gulfood 2026, T57 signed 150 MoUs and Letters of Intent with institutional buyers, including
Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF), Grandiose, Al Amir Food Industries, Casa Alhambra, Damaco Group, Rancheiro, Sura Trading, Sengheng Noodle Company (Rabbit Noodle), MAFI for Agricultural Produce Industries, and Xinxiang Koukou Miao Food Co., Ltd., among others. These are not conference badge swaps or newsletter sign-ups; each MoU required legal review and internal approval within organizations that, by design, are cautious and committee-driven.
In a typical B2B SaaS funnel, only a small fraction of top‑of‑funnel leads ever reach this level of commitment. Benchmarks for B2B SaaS lead‑to‑customer conversion rates of around 1–5%, even for well‑run teams. By contrast, T57’s Gulfood MoUs represent buyers who have already crossed several internal gates: they have acknowledged a problem, aligned multiple stakeholders, and authorized their leadership teams to formalize intent before product launch. That is no longer “awareness”; it is pre‑qualified demand. The world is telling us to hurry up and launch.
From intent to paid subscriptions

From intent to paid subscriptions
Institutional buyers rarely attach their signatures to speculative ideas. Many of T57’s counterparts have gone further, requesting beta access and pilot agreements ahead of our November 2026 beta. This matters because conversion rates rise sharply when engagement precedes sales outreach. A study of B2B buying groups found that accounts with prior engagement converted to pipeline at up to 22.88%, substantially higher when compared with cold outreach.
T57’s Gulfood MoUs sit firmly in an ‘engaged, committee‑approved’ category. They are, in effect, reliable intent signals that we expect to translate into a disproportionately high paid‑subscription conversion rate within 90 days of launch. By the time our platform acquires its next set of features, these organizations will have lived with T57 in pilots, validated workflows across trade, logistics, compliance, and finance, and socialized the platform internally. The sales question will then shift from “Why T57?” to “How fast can we roll this out across markets?”
A structurally different acquisition engine

A structurally different acquisition engine
For most SaaS companies, growth depends on sustained spending to generate and convert cold leads. Industry data suggests average customer acquisition costs (CAC) for B2B SaaS are in the hundreds of dollars per customer, with typical ‘lead to win’ rates under 5% and CAC payback periods stretching to a year or more. That model is capital‑intensive and fragile when markets tighten.
T57’s Gulfood‑driven pipeline looks structurally different.
The 150 MoUs are not anonymous leads but named, institution‑level prospects with multi‑stakeholder buy‑in.
The acquisition cost per MoU is effectively amortized across a single, high‑density event rather than scattered across diffuse digital channels.
Each MoU sits inside a category—retail, dairy, manufacturing, specialty food—that can anchor expansion into adjacent accounts once value is demonstrated.
If conventional SaaS funnels are pyramids, T57’s Gulfood pipeline is more like a column: narrower at the top, but with a far higher proportion expected to convert at the bottom. We will still invest in classic go-to-market motions (partner channels, targeted campaigns, etc.), but they will be layered on top of a core of committed, high-intent institutional buyers.
Why the world is ready for T57

Why the world is ready for T57
The strength of this demand must be understood against the backdrop of the global food trade. Food supply chains are growing more complex, spanning multiple jurisdictions, logistics regimes, and regulatory systems. The launch of dedicated events such as Gulfood Logistics underscores how critical integrated, resilient supply chains have become to both exporters and import‑dependent economies.
Across conversations at Gulfood, industry leaders repeated the same frustrations: fragmented systems, manual processes, delayed deals, and compliance bottlenecks. These are not marginal inefficiencies; they are structural frictions that inflate costs, slow response to shocks, and constrain growth at a time when demand and climate risk are both rising.
T57 is designed as an AI-native food trade operating system, precisely for this environment. It brings together trade execution, logistics, compliance, finance, and data on a single, intelligent platform. The resonance of that proposition at Gulfood suggests that the industry is not merely curious about new tools; it is actively seeking foundational infrastructure for how food trade will operate in the next decade.
From early traction to durable growth

From early traction to durable growth Investor benchmarks increasingly view strong pre‑order or pre‑launch demand as a leading indicator of durable growth. When a Nation Becomes Your Customer: Inside the Race to Sell AI to India’s Farms

When a Nation Becomes Your Customer: Inside the Race to Sell AI to India’s Farms
India’s Digital Agriculture Mission and the push for traceable public investment in farming.
Umme Habeeba Khanum Chief Marketing Officer
4 May 2026 5 min read
The first time the words “11 crore farmers” (110 million) appeared in a project review, the marketer in me did a double-take. This was not the usual TAM slide. This was the Government of India’s target for creating digital farmer identities by 2026–27 under the Digital Agriculture Mission (DAM). As Chief Marketing Officer of T57, I realized something profound: for once, the buyer's ambition was bigger than the startup's.
T57 is not creating a mere SaaS platform. We were creating a way for a nation to see, understand, and serve millions of small farmers, who make up about 86% of India’s landholdings, yet control less than half the crop area. That changes everything about how you think about positioning, storytelling, and proof.
What happens when your “segment” is 11 crore farmers?

What happens when your “segment” is 11 crore farmers?
Most B2B stories begin with a niche. Ours begins with a policy. DAM, approved with an outlay of ₹2,817 crore, is building digital public infrastructure for agriculture: AgriStack for farmer identities, a Digital Crop Survey covering all districts by 2025–26, and decision-support systems that can ingest everything from soil data to scheme payments. The mission’s north star is clear—every rupee of public investment should be traceable to a farmer, a plot, and a crop.
By 2025, more than 6.1 crore farmers already had Aadhaar-like digital IDs linked to land records across 14 states. The target is 11 crore IDs, backed by a nationwide digital crop survey, within a tight three-year window.
For a platform like T57, this is not “market potential”; this is infrastructure being laid at speed; this is the infrastructure on which entrepreneurs and startups can build products and services that propel the agriculture sector. My job as a marketer is to show how T57 can be the intelligence layer that rides on these rails, turning identity, land, and crop data into decisions.
If the farmer is changing, how must our story change?

If the farmer is changing, how must our story change?
Beneath the headline numbers lies a more human truth. India’s agriculture is powered by farmers with less than two hectares of land, who own just about 47% of the crop area. They are vulnerable to climate shocks and price volatility, yet 84% of marginal farmers say they do not want to quit farming, despite low profits and natural calamities. That stubborn commitment is both a moral argument and a strategic brief.
On the other side of the equation, access has quietly transformed. As of April 2024, around 95.15% of India’s 6.44 lakh villages had 3G/4G mobile connectivity, and rural internet subscribers stood at roughly 398 million. The story is no longer “Can farmers come online?” It is “Can we justify not using data and AI to serve them better when the pipes already exist?” For T57, this is the pivot: we do not market AI as magic; we market it as overdue infrastructure for people who have stayed in agriculture even when the odds said leave.
How do you market to a government that thinks like a platform company?

How do you market to a government that thinks like a platform company?
DAM reads less like a traditional scheme and more like a platform roadmap. It specifies components (farmer IDs, Digital Crop Survey, decision-support systems) and milestones (6 crore IDs in FY 2024–25, 3 crore in 2025–26, 2 crore in 2026–27). This is exactly how any serious product team would frame a multi-year build.
So we have begun to think of the Government of India the way we would treat the world’s largest enterprise client. That means marketing T57 not as a standalone app, but as a DPI-native capability:
Built to ingest farmer IDs, plot-level crop data, and soil profiles from AgriStack and DAM systems.
Designed to give district officials dashboards that translate model outputs into crisp signals: which blocks are at risk, which FPOs to support, which schemes to tweak.
Equipped with governance features—explainable models, audit trails, and data lineage—because public money demands public justification.
Instead of saying “We can predict yield,” our message to the Government of India is, “We create a global network that amplifies the impact of the data.”
Can a pilot be both a product experiment and a political story?

Can a pilot be both a product experiment and a political story?
In fast-growing tech companies, pilots are designed to test features. In Indian agriculture, pilots must also test narratives. DAM’s timelines—such as completing a Digital Crop Survey across all districts by 2025–26—are political commitments as much as technical ones.
This pushed T57 to rethink its proof strategy. Each pilot district needed one storyline a minister could use to inspire everyone, backed by hard numbers:
A district where AI-driven advisories helped farmers maintain yields in a year of erratic rainfall, compared to neighboring blocks still relying on traditional advisories.
A command area where irrigation guidance, layered on soil and weather data, reduced water use per hectare with no loss in output.
A subsidy programme where linking farmer IDs to T57 analytics improved targeting efficiency and reduced leakages.
In each case, the KPI is not “model accuracy.” It is “Can this story survive a question on the floor of Parliament?” That bar forces us to build marketing around measurable, defensible outcomes.
What does it mean to call a nation your design partner?

What does it mean to call a nation your design partner?
Perhaps the most unexpected shift for me, as CMO, has been cultural. When a country commits to giving 11 crore farmers digital IDs and connecting over 95% of its villages, you are not just selling into a market—you are becoming part of a national redesign project.
That comes with responsibility. T57’s marketing must signal interoperability, respect for data governance, and a bias for capacity-building inside government, not just platform lock-in. It must acknowledge constraints—small holdings, climate risk, literacy gaps—while showing how AI can make the system more forgiving, not more brittle, for the 86% who farm small plots and still choose to stay on the land.
The exciting prospect of marketing T57 to the Government of India, then, is not merely the addressable market. It is the chance to help my country turn raw connectivity, new digital identities, and decades of farmer resilience into a more intelligent, more responsive agricultural brain. I am looking forward to this opportunity in the coming months.

When Food Trade Deals Happen Before the Handshake

When Food Trade Deals Happen Before the Handshake
Why discovery and contracting are moving from trade-show floors to AI-native trade platforms.
Afzal Hussain Mohammed Nakheeb Founder, Chairman & Head of Strategy
20 Apr 2026 6 min read
One morning at Gulfood 2026, a mid-sized Dubai-based distributor told me something I had never heard framed so starkly: “My real Gulfood happens after Gulfood.” The booth at the Gulfood event, the product samples, the meetings, the business cards—all of that, he said, was just “the trailer.” The actual movie was the multi-month grind of background checks, cautious trial orders, delayed payments, and endless negotiation before a relationship becomes truly trusted.” The most critical part of the agri and food trade still moves at the pace of intuition, while the industry is obsessed with speed and wants fresh produce and just-in-time logistics. I think digital platforms can change that.
What is the invisible tax on trust?

What is the invisible tax on trust? Across conversations at Gulfood 2026, one pattern repeated: it takes multi-months, sometimes years, for buyers and suppliers to truly verify, qualify, and trust each other. That lag is not about a lack of intent; it is about a lack of structured, shared intelligence about who is on the other side of the table: their capacity, compliance, financial behavior, and operational discipline. In effect, every new relationship pays a “trust tax” in time and missed opportunities. Traditional trade shows were never designed to solve this. They are powerful for: Spotting trends and categories. Meeting a dense network of people in a short span. Signaling ambition through presence and branding. But they are structurally weak at: Verifying counterparties at scale. Embedding finance and risk tools into every conversation. Translating meetings into executable, low-friction deals. Participants pay top dollar for booths, banners, logistics, product samples, travel, visiting cards, and stays, only to see many conversations stall because neither side can underwrite the other’s risk. Larger buyers often ask for credit; smaller or mid-sized suppliers cannot extend it without trust and visibility into the real quality of the counterparty. According to most private estimates, the success rate of deals is far lower than the event's intensity would suggest.
What is the invisible tax on trust?
The result is a misallocation of capital: we over-invest in moments of visibility and under-invest in the systems that make those moments actionable.
When offline friction meets digital readiness

When offline friction meets digital readiness The question is not whether trade shows have value; they do. But the question is whether they should remain the primary engine of discovery, trust-building, and deal-making in global food trade. Three shifts make it imperative that we rethink this model: Data is finally abundant – but fragmented. Exporters, distributors, and retailers are sitting on operational, logistics, and sales data that, in theory, can answer questions like “Is matcha growing faster than boba tea in South Asia?” and “At what price points do volumes break?” Yet most companies lack the AI tools and shared infrastructure to turn this into collective market intelligence. Trust has become the new infrastructure. Regulators, financiers, and corporates expect continuous KYC/KYB, provenance, compliance evidence, and ratings, not one-time checks. That kind of always-on verification is impossible to do manually across thousands of counterparties, but it is exactly what digital, AI-led systems are good at. Trade corridors are being rewired at scale. From the Digital Silk Road for food security to new sovereign agri corridors across Asia, Africa, and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), governments and institutions are actively seeking digital rails for food and agri trade.
When offline friction meets digital readiness

The opportunity is not just to digitize forms; it is to create new, trusted routes that enable verified participants to move goods and credit with minimal friction. In this context, relying on episodic, physical events as the backbone of trade discovery looks increasingly like a structural blind spot.
How can virtual trade events start from trust rather than visibility?

How can virtual trade events start from trust rather than visibility?
This is where T57’s approach diverges from the conventional idea of “virtual events.”
Most virtual trade shows try to replicate the expo floor online – digital booths, chat windows, and scheduled video calls. They digitized the surface, not the substance.
T57 inverts the sequence. It starts with:
Continuous AI-led KYC/KYB that verifies, scores, and monitors every participant (farmers, cooperatives, traders, logistics providers, retailers, banks, and governments) before they transact.
Embedded trade finance and settlement tools, from near-instant letters of credit to digital and tokenized instruments, that are woven into the trade flow.
End-to-end traceability and compliance using blockchain-backed records that give financiers, insurers, and regulators confidence in every shipment.
On top of this trust and execution layer, T57 can host virtual trade events where:
Every counterparty is already verified and scored.
Financing options are visible at the point of negotiation.
Logistics, pricing, and market intelligence are integrated into the conversation.
A multi-month trust-building process collapses into a set of machine-verified checks that run in seconds. Instead of exchanging business cards and “keeping in touch,” participants can move directly to structuring real, financeable deals.
How can T57 become the new trade show for agri and food?

How can T57 become the new trade show for agri and food? Seen this way, T57 is not just an online marketplace; it is a programmable trade environment that can absorb many of the high-value functions of a physical trade show and extend them year-round. Here is how it can effectively replace the traditional trade show workflow for agri and food: Discovery without noise. Buyers can search for suppliers by verified attributes (certifications, capacity, past performance, pricing behavior, etc.) rather than booth location or brand familiarity. Smaller and emerging brands, which may never secure a prime trade-show slot, can surface on merit, not marketing spend. Structured, data-rich conversations. Instead of speculative talks, participants engage with live data: demand signals from retailers, surplus-deficit alerts across regions, price corridors, and logistics constraints. A retailer in Riyadh can assess whether to source directly from a processor in Vietnam with a clear view of demand, prices, and shipping realities, without waiting for next year’s expo. Embedded execution. Once intent is established, trade finance, documentation, risk mitigation, and settlement are all triggered within the same platform. This removes the traditional gap between “we met at Gulfood” and “we finally closed our first shipment,” which can run into years. Continuous, AI-driven relationship building.
How can T57 become the new trade show for agri and food?

Performance data, payment behavior, and logistics reliability feed back into the trust score over time. Instead of anecdotal impressions gathered in hallways, counterparties build algorithmically augmented reputations. At Gulfood 2026, the Letters of Intent T57 signed with retailers, brands, and distributors were less about a single event and more about building these always-on corridors of visibility, trade, and finance across regions such as the Middle East, Europe, and Southeast Asia. The pattern is clear: institutions want their “real Gulfood” – the months of trust work – to happen on a platform, not on the sidelines.
An invitation to step into the post-expo era

An invitation to step into the post-expo era
Trade shows will not disappear; they will be redefined. They will become places to deepen relationships, signal strategic intent, and convene stakeholders. They will not be the primary engine for stitching together trust, finance, and execution.
That engine will be digital, data-rich, and AI-native. T57 is being built as that engine: a trusted corridor where verified buyers and suppliers can discover each other, understand real demand, access embedded finance, and move from conversation to contract without the multi-month tax.
For founders, CEOs, and trade leaders in the agri-food industry, the question is no longer whether to attend the next big expo. The question is: where will your real Gulfood happen?
If the answer is still “in spreadsheets, messages, and offline negotiations after the event,” the opportunity cost is already visible in your margins. If, instead, you choose to make T57 your default environment for discovery and execution, the trade show becomes what it was always meant to be: not the movie, but the trailer, for deals that are already structurally possible the moment you log in.
